title: Complex plane, modulus and polar form

beats.say: A real number lives on a line. A complex number needs two coordinates.

do.text: From the real line to the complex plane.

beats.say: The number i is defined by i squared equals negative one.
In rectangular form, write z as a plus b i; a and b are real numbers.
The real part, a, is horizontal. The imaginary part, b, is vertical.

do.text: Real part: across. Imaginary part: up or down.

beats.say: So a plus b i is the point a, b. The coefficient b is a real number; i marks the imaginary direction.
In particular, i sits one unit above zero.
Point P represents z. Write z in the form a plus b i.

do.text: Point $P$ represents $z$. Write $z$ in the form $a+bi$.

beats.say: Three left: the real part is negative three.
Two up: the imaginary part is positive two.
Negative three plus two i. Check the choices against the picture: left, then up.
P represents z; Q represents w. Choose z plus w.

do.text: Points $P$ and $Q$ represent $z$ and $w$. Choose $z+w$.

beats.say: Read each arrow from zero: z is three plus i. w is negative one plus two i.
Adding means following both arrows. Slide a copy of w to the tip of z.

do.text: Add arrows tip to tail.

beats.say: The copy still goes one left and two up. Its length and direction have not changed.

do.text: The same arrow, starting at $P$.

beats.say: The sum runs from zero to the final tip.
Horizontally: three plus negative one is two.
Vertically: one plus two is three. Combine matching parts.
The answer is two plus three i. The endpoint checks both parts: two right, three up.
The modulus of z means its distance from zero. The bars around z name that distance.
Across and up form the legs of a right triangle. The direct distance is its hypotenuse.
Pythagoras gives the distance squared. Take the nonnegative square root to get the distance.
Find the modulus of negative two plus four i, in simplest exact form.

do.text: Find $|-2+4i|$ in simplest exact form.

beats.say: The legs have lengths two and four. A negative coordinate does not make a negative length.
Call the distance r. Square each coordinate, then add: four plus sixteen is twenty.
Take the square root. Twenty is four times five, so a factor of two comes outside.
Check: the straight path is longer than four, but shorter than the two-leg path, six.
There is another way to locate the same point: distance and direction.

do.meaning: Locate a point by distance $r$ and angle $\theta$.

beats.say: The distance r is the radius. Start the angle at the positive real axis, pointing right.
Turn counterclockwise. The swept angle is theta, also called the argument.

do.text: Angle $\theta$: counterclockwise from the positive real axis.

beats.say: Drop a vertical line to the real axis. The radius becomes the hypotenuse of a right triangle.
Cosine is horizontal divided by radius. So the real part is r times cosine theta.
Sine is vertical divided by radius. So the imaginary part is r times sine theta.
Put those parts into a plus b i, and factor out r.
Both forms land on this same point. Rectangular gives the components; polar gives length and direction.

do.text: Same point. Two ways to name it.

beats.say: Beyond the first quadrant, cosine and sine are signed coordinates. Here, left makes cosine negative; up makes sine positive.

do.text: Left: $a<0$. Up: $b>0$.

beats.say: For exact values, use the special right triangles. A thirty-degree triangle has hypotenuse two and short leg one.

do.text: Exact values come from special right triangles.

beats.say: Pythagoras gives the other leg: square root of three.
At thirty degrees, cosine is root three over two; sine is one half.
At sixty degrees, the opposite and adjacent legs switch roles, so those two values switch.
At forty-five degrees, the legs are equal. Legs one and one give hypotenuse square root of two.
Both ratios are one over root two, or root two over two. The quadrant supplies the signs.

do.text: Use the triangle for sizes; the quadrant for signs.

beats.say: Write this polar number in rectangular form, a plus b i.

do.text: Write $4(\cos\frac{5\pi}{6}+i\sin\frac{5\pi}{6})$ as $a+bi$.

beats.say: The radius is four. The angle is five pi over six.
Angles here use radians: pi is a half-turn, one hundred eighty degrees.

do.text: A half-turn: $\pi$ radians $=180^\circ$.

beats.say: Five pi over six is one hundred fifty degrees. Turn from the positive real axis.
The point is left and up. The real part must be negative; the imaginary part, positive. Reject choices in other quadrants.

do.text: Left and up: $a<0$, $b>0$.

beats.say: The reference angle is the acute angle to the real axis: thirty degrees.
Cosine is negative root three over two. Multiply by four for the horizontal part.
Sine is one half. Multiply by four for the vertical part: two.
So z is negative two root three plus two i.
Check: left and up, with a larger horizontal part. Swapping sine and cosine would miss this point.

do.text: Cosine gives the real part. Sine gives the imaginary part.

beats.say: Call the reference angle alpha. In quadrant one, theta equals alpha.

do.text: Reference angle $\alpha$: the acute angle to the real axis.

beats.say: Left and up: quadrant two. Subtract alpha from a half-turn.
Left and down: quadrant three. Go past a half-turn by alpha.
Right and down: quadrant four. Stop alpha short of a full turn.
Write two minus two root three i in polar form.

do.text: Write $2-2\sqrt3i$ in polar form. Use $r>0,\ 0\le\theta<2\pi$.

beats.say: Use positive radius, and an angle from zero up to, but not including, two pi.

do.text: $r>0$, $0\le\theta<2\pi$.

beats.say: Reread the signs: right and down. That is quadrant four.

do.text: Quadrant IV: $a>0$, $b<0$.

beats.say: First, the radius. Square both parts: four plus twelve is sixteen.
The radius is four. Both forms must reach this same circle.
Divide each component by four. Cosine is two over four: one half.
Sine is negative two root three over four: negative root three over two.
Their sizes give a reference angle of pi over three, or sixty degrees.
But pi over three points up. We need down. The reference angle alone is not the answer.

do.text: Choose the quadrant first. Then use the reference angle.

beats.say: A full turn is two pi. Stop pi over three short of that full turn.
That gives five pi over three, in the requested interval.
A clockwise angle of negative pi over three reaches the same point, but falls outside that interval.

do.text: $-\pi/3$ points correctly, but $0\le\theta<2\pi$ requires $5\pi/3$.

beats.say: Use radius four and angle five pi over three in both places.
Check by converting back: four times one half is two; four times negative root three over two is negative two root three.
Points on the axes work too. A real number has imaginary part zero.

do.text: Axis points: number, then angle in parentheses.

beats.say: A purely imaginary number has real part zero. Its arrow is vertical.
The negative real axis is angle pi. Straight down is three pi over two.

do.text: Axis angles: $0,\ \pi/2,\ \pi,\ 3\pi/2$.

beats.say: At zero itself, the modulus is zero. There is no direction, so its argument is undefined.

do.text: Zero has no defined argument.

beats.say: Read what is requested. The picture tells you which quantities matter.

do.text: Read the requested form and angle interval.

beats.say: Components locate the point. Their signs fix its quadrant.

do.text: Components locate the point and fix its quadrant.

beats.say: Distance comes from the right triangle. Direction comes from cosine and sine together.

do.text: Find the length, then match both signed components.

beats.say: Use the requested angle interval. Convert back to check.

do.text: Use the requested angle interval. Convert back to check.
